entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9931"/><div sID="gen17645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9931"/><hi type="bold">7. fan--</hi>tribulation--from tribulum, a threshing instrument, which separates the chaff from the wheat (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen17645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gates of the land--</hi>that is, the extreme bounds of the land through which the entrance to and exit from it lie. Maurer translates, "I will fan," that is, cast them forth "to the gates of the land" (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.13">Na 3:13</reference>). "In the gates"; English Version draws the image from a man cleaning corn with a fan; he stands at the gate of the threshing-floor in the open air, to remove the wheat from the chaff by means of the wind; so God threatens to remove Israel out of the bounds of the land [Houbigant]. <div eID="gen17646" type="x-p"/>

Verily--</hi>literally, "Shall it not be?" that is, "Surely it shall be."<div eID="gen17660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy remnant--</hi>the final issue of thy life; thy life, which now seems to thee so sad, shall eventuate in prosperity [Calvin]. They who think that they shall be the surviving remnant, whereas thou shalt perish, shall themselves fall, whereas thou shalt remain and be favored by the conquerors [Junius], (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.4">Jr 40:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.11">39:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.12">12</reference>). The Keri reads, "I will set thee free (or as Maurer, 'I will establish thee') for good" (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">Jr 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.8.22">Ezr 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.122">Psa 119:122</reference>).<div eID="gen17661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to entreat thee well--</hi>literally, "to meet thee"; so "to be placable, nay, of their own accord to anticipate in meeting thee with kindness" [Calvin]. I prefer this translation as according with the event (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.11">Jr 39:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.4">40:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.5">5</reference>). Gesenius, from <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jr 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.18">27:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.15">Job 21:15</reference>, translates (not only will I relieve thee from the enemy's vexations, but) "I will make thine enemy (that now vexeth thee) apply to thee with prayers" (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.14">Jr 38:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.42.2-Jer.42.6">42:2-6</reference>). <div eID="gen17662" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 11. Verily-- literally, "Shall it not be?" that is, "Surely it shall be." thy remnant-- the final issue of thy life; thy life, which now seems to thee so sad, shall eventuate in prosperity [Calvin]. They who think that they shall be the surviving remnant, whereas thou shalt perish, shall themselves fall, whereas thou shalt remain and be favored by the conquerors [Junius], ( Jr 40:4 , 5 ; 39:11 , 12 ). The Keri reads, "I will set thee free (or as Maurer, 'I will establish thee') for good" ( Jr 14:11 ; Ezr 8:22 ; Psa 119:122 ). to entreat thee well-- literally, "to meet thee"; so "to be placable, nay, of their own accord to anticipate in meeting thee with kindness" [Calvin]. I prefer this translation as according with the event ( Jr 39:11 , 12 ; 40:4 , 5 ). Gesenius, from Jr 7:16 ; 27:18 ; Job 21:15 , translates (not only will I relieve thee from the enemy's vexations, but) "I will make thine enemy (that now vexeth thee) apply to thee with prayers" ( Jr 38:14 ; 42:2-6 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9936"/><div sID="gen17663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9936"/><hi type="bold">12. steel--</hi>rather, brass or copper, which mixed with "iron" (by the Chalybes near the Euxine Pontus, far north of Palestine), formed the hardest metal, like our steel. Can the Jews, hardy like common iron though they be, break the still hardier Chaldees of the north (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.14">Jr 1:14</reference>), who resemble the Chalybian iron hardened with copper? Certainly not [Calvin]. Henderson translates. "Can one break iron, (even) the northern iron, and brass," on the ground that English Version makes ordinary iron not so hard as brass. But it is not brass, but a particular mixture of iron and brass, which is represented as harder than common iron, which was probably then of inferior texture, owing to ignorance of modern modes of preparation. <div eID="gen17663" type="x-p"/>

Thy substance ... sins--</hi>Judea's, not Jeremiah's.<div eID="gen17664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without price--</hi>God casts His people away as a thing worth naught (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.12">Psa 44:12</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9941"/><div sID="gen17676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9941"/>17. My "rejoicing" (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.16">Jr 15:16</reference>) was not that of the profane mockers (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>; 26:4, 5) at feasts. So far from having fellowship with these, he was expelled from society, and made to sit "alone," because of his faithful prophecies.<div eID="gen17676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of thy hand--</hi>that is, Thine inspiration (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.11">Is 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.3">Eze 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.14">3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen17677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filled me with indignation--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Jer.6.11">Jr 6:11</reference>, "full of the fury of the Lord"; so full was he of the subject (God's "indignation" against the ungodly) with which God had inspired him, as not to be able to contain himself from expressing it. The same comparison by contrast between the effect of inspiration, and that of wine, both taking a man out of himself, occurs (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.13">Ac 2:13</reference>, 15, 18). <div eID="gen17678" type="x-p"/>

The same comparison by contrast between the effect of inspiration, and that of wine, both taking a man out of himself, occurs ( Ac 2:13 , 15, 18).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9942"/><div sID="gen17679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9942"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.15">Jr 30:15</reference>). "Pain," namely, the perpetual persecution to which he was exposed, and his being left by God without consolation and "alone." Contrast his feeling here with that in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.16">Jr 15:16</reference>, when he enjoyed the full presence of God, and was inspired by His words. Therefore he utters words of his natural "infirmity" (so David, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.10">Psa 77:10</reference>) here; as before he spoke under the higher spiritual nature given him.<div eID="gen17679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a liar, and as--</hi>rather, "as a deceiving (river) ... waters that are not sure (lasting)"; opposed to "living (perennial) waters" (<reference osisRef="Job.6.15">Job 6:15</reference>). Streams that the thirsty traveller had calculated on being full in winter, but which disappoint him in his sorest need, having run dry in the heat of summer. Jehovah had promised Jeremiah protection from his enemies (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.18">Jr 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>); his infirmity suggests that God had failed to do so. <div eID="gen17680" type="x-p"/>

God's reply to Jeremiah.<div eID="gen17681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return ... bring ... again--</hi>Jeremiah, by his impatient language, had left his proper posture towards God; God saith, "If thou wilt return (to thy former patient discharge of thy prophetic function) I will bring thee back" to thy former position: in the Hebrew there is a play of words, "return ... turn again" (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jr 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.1">4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen17682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand before me--</hi>minister acceptably to Me (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.8">De 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.1">1Ki 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.15">18:15</reference>).<div eID="gen17683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take ... precious from ... vile--</hi>image from metals: "If thou wilt separate what is precious in thee (the divine graces imparted) from what is vile (thy natural corruptions, impatience, and hasty words), thou shall be as My mouth": my mouthpiece (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.16">Ex 4:16</reference>).<div eID="gen17684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return not thou unto them--</hi>Let not them lead you into their profane ways (as Jeremiah had spoken irreverently, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.18">Jr 15:18</reference>), but lead thou them to the ways of godliness (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.16">Jr 15:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.17">17</reference>). <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.26">Eze 22:26</reference> accords with the other interpretation, which, however, does not so well suit the context, "If thou wilt separate from the promiscuous mass the better ones, and lead them to conversion by faithful warnings," &c. <div eID="gen17685" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 19. God's reply to Jeremiah. return ... bring ... again-- Jeremiah, by his impatient language, had left his proper posture towards God; God saith, "If thou wilt return (to thy former patient discharge of thy prophetic function) I will bring thee back" to thy former position: in the Hebrew there is a play of words, "return ... turn again" ( Jr 8:4 ; 4:1 ). stand before me-- minister acceptably to Me ( De 10:8 ; 1Ki 17:1 ; 18:15 ). take ... precious from ... vile-- image from metals: "If thou wilt separate what is precious in thee (the divine graces imparted) from what is vile (thy natural corruptions, impatience, and hasty words), thou shall be as My mouth": my mouthpiece ( Ex 4:16 ). return not thou unto them-- Let not them lead you into their profane ways (as Jeremiah had spoken irreverently, Jr 15:18 ), but lead thou them to the ways of godliness ( Jr 15:16 , 17 ). Eze 22:26 accords with the other interpretation, which, however, does not so well suit the context, "If thou wilt separate from the promiscuous mass the better ones, and lead them to conversion by faithful warnings," &c.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9944"/><div sID="gen17686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9944"/>20-21. The promise of <reference osisRef="Jer.1.18">Jr 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>, in almost the same words, but with the addition, adapted to the present attacks of Jeremiah's formidable enemies, "I will deliver thee out of ... wicked ... redeem ... terrible"; the repetition is in order to assure Jeremiah that God is the same now as when He first made the promise, in opposition to the prophet's irreverent accusation of unfaithfulness (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.18">Jr 15:18</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.15"/>
